27	cells cannot read another cell's private data to assemble those features.
28	
29	Projects store a jurisdiction in `Project.Region`, but not an explicit processing
30	cell. ProjectDirectory derives a cluster slug only when exactly one serving
31	cluster matches that jurisdiction. A jurisdiction is not a cell. Adding a cluster
32	must not change the home of existing project data.
33	
34	GitHub mirror creation already uses one system-managed project per upstream
35	owner, across all cells. Its existing region reflects the request that first
36	created the project. That value is not evidence of an intentional processing home.
37	
38	## Decision
39	
40	### The project owns processing placement
41	
42	A project has one explicit primary processing cell, recorded by the control
43	plane. The cell must satisfy the project's jurisdiction and residency rules.
44	The assignment exists independently of repo membership, including for an empty
45	project.
46	
47	The project's authoritative non-Git data lives in this cell. Each owned repo
48	group's authoritative non-Git data lives there too. Work that produces or changes
49	that authoritative state runs there. This includes project trails, repo activity,
50	and authoritative search indices.
51	
52	The owning project is the only placement authority for a repo group. A reference
53	from another project does not confer ownership or change placement.
54	
55	### Repo groups select a local processing placement
56	
57	A group's processing-primary placement must belong to its project's processing
58	cell. It identifies the local placement that performs the group's work; it does
59	not define an independent processing home.
60	
61	Each repo group needs a usable Git placement in that cell. Creation, adoption,
62	reconciliation, and admin overrides must preserve this rule. Replica creation in
63	another cell must not reassign the group or change its processing home.
64	
65	The assigned cell and processing availability are separate states. When no local
66	placement can process a repo, the assignment remains unchanged. The system reports
67	processing as unavailable or pending. It does not elect a placement in another
68	cell merely because that placement has a healthy Git copy.
69	
70	Project-only operations do not depend on the health or existence of a particular
71	repo placement. Replica maintenance can still run in each replica's own cell.
72	
73	### Git-data primaries remain separate
74	
75	| Concept | Authority |
76	| --- | --- |
77	| Primary processing cell | Project |
78	| Processing-primary placement for the group | Repo group |
79	| Canonical Git source | Repo group's Git-data primary |
80	
81	For GitHub mirrors, GitHub remains the Git-data primary. A mirror in the project's
82	cell supplies local Git data for processing. Other mirrors remain valid placements.
83	
84	New native repos start in their project's processing cell. Their initial Git-data
85	primary is therefore local, but Git authority and processing authority remain
86	distinct. This decision does not promote an existing native replica or change an
87	existing native Git-data primary. Native-primary promotion requires its own safe
88	handover, as described in the [native mirroring ADR](20260720-native-mirroring.md).
89	
90	### Project kinds and permissions stay separate
91	
92	Native projects contain native repo groups. GitHub mirrors projects contain
93	GitHub repo groups. Placement inheritance applies to both kinds without combining
94	their permission models.
95	
96	Under this decision, each owner-scoped mirrors project has one processing cell
97	for all its repo groups. Additional Git placements do not create additional
98	project owners.
99	
100	This decision grants no new access. GitHub-derived repo permissions remain in
101	force. Permission to create a mirror does not grant permission to relocate its
102	project. Authorization for project-level features remains a separate contract;
103	co-location alone never authorizes access to another repo's data.
104	
105	### Assignment changes require migration
106	
107	A project cell change is a data migration, not an ordinary metadata edit.
108	Reassigning a repo group to a project in another cell also requires migration.
109	The initial implementation does not provide general-purpose transfer or automatic
110	cross-cell failover.
111	
112	Routing for authoritative non-Git operations follows the project assignment.
113	A fallback suitable for a Git read cannot select the destination for an
114	authoritative non-Git write. Unknown or unavailable placement must not cause a
115	write in an arbitrary cell.
116	
117	Future non-Git replication can add copies outside the primary cell. Replication
118	does not itself grant write authority. A future promotion or multi-writer protocol
119	must define data readiness, conflict handling, and protection against stale writers.
120	
121	## Future extension: project placement policy
122	
123	The project can later define a broader placement policy for its repo groups.
124	This can cover primary placement and the regions or cells available for
125	additional placements:
126	
127	- The primary processing cell.
128	- The placement of native Git-data primaries, independently of processing primaries.
129	- The regions and cells in which Git replicas or future non-Git replicas are permitted.
130	
131	GitHub remains the canonical Git source for GitHub mirrors. Project policy governs
132	Entire placements; it does not relocate an external forge's Git-data primary.
133	
134	An available location permits placement; it does not require a replica there.
135	Policy must respect residency constraints. Changing policy does not itself move
136	data or promote a primary. Existing placements need an explicit reconciliation
137	and migration path when they no longer satisfy the policy.
138	
139	This is an extension point, not part of the initial implementation. The current
140	decision establishes project-owned processing placement without adding a general
141	placement-policy system.
142	
143	## Migration and compatibility
144	
145	The invariant is independent of the existing placement inventory. A read-only
146	analysis informs rollout; it does not gate this architectural decision.
147	
148	Existing mirrors projects can have disjoint placement sets. One repo might exist
149	only in US and another only in EU. Migration must choose an explicit destination
150	and add any missing Git placements there. Existing replicas can remain.
151	
152	> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
153	> New mirrors projects use US regardless of owner residency. Existing projects still require explicit migration decisions.
154	
155	A cell with a complete Git placement set is a useful candidate, not necessarily
156	the owner's preferred destination. US is not a mandatory home. Destination
157	selection must respect residency requirements and account for the lack of a
158	self-service transfer operation. The existing race-selected region is not a
159	sufficient basis for that choice.
160	
161	A complete Git placement set does not imply complete non-Git state. A fresh clone
162	cannot recover trails or other authoritative application records. Migration must
163	locate that state, transfer it safely, and verify it before activating the new
164	home. Derived data can be rebuilt only where its source is complete.
165	
166	A primary-pointer update and a best-effort announcement do not constitute a safe
167	handover. Cutover must prevent old workers and writers from continuing against the
168	previous home. Migration must use an authorized transfer mechanism without relaxing
169	normal cell isolation. Source deletion follows verification and the recovery policy.
170	
171	Deploy compatible schema and consumers before enforcing the assignment. Track
172	legacy projects explicitly during rollout. Features that require project-wide
173	locality remain disabled until the project and its repo groups satisfy the rule.
174	Changes in cluster topology must not silently relocate a project.
175	
176	A code rollback must preserve the assignment and the active data home. Code that
177	can elect an out-of-cell primary is not safe after cutover. Operators must retain
178	a verified recovery path rather than treat a schema rollback as data recovery.
179	
180	## Consequences
181	
182	- Project-level features can access owned repo data within one cell.
183	- A project becomes a unit of processing placement and correlated availability.
184	- Large mirrors projects concentrate authoritative processing in one cell.
185	- Missing home placements add Git storage and replication traffic.
186	- Git replicas elsewhere do not provide non-Git failover by themselves.
187	- Cross-project references do not solve cross-cell reads or authorization.
188	- Placement remains explicit as additional cells and replication modes appear.
189	
190	## Alternatives considered
191	
192	**Use the project cell only as a default.** Rejected. Repo overrides and automatic
193	re-election would recreate the locality mismatch.
194	
195	**Resolve the cell from jurisdiction on each request.** Rejected. A jurisdiction
196	can contain multiple cells. Infrastructure changes must not redefine data ownership.
197	
198	**Allow cross-cell reads for project features.** Rejected for this design. That
199	would weaken cell independence and introduce a distributed dependency for local work.
200	
201	> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
202	> US is mandatory for new mirrors projects. This does not relocate existing projects or constrain additional Git placements.
203	
204	**Put every GitHub mirror in US permanently.** Not selected. US can be a migration
205	candidate where permitted, but it is not an architectural requirement.
206	
207	## Delivery
208	
209	The [Linear project](https://linear.app/entirehq/project/projects-define-primary-processing-cell-and-placement-rules-bd55ec1c3cb9/overview)
210	tracks implementation slices, consumer coordination, migration analysis, destination
211	selection, transfer tooling, verification, and rollout. This ADR records the
212	invariant and compatibility requirements, not the execution plan.
213	
214	Related decisions:
215	
216	- [Every repo belongs to a repo group](20260715-repo-group-for-every-repo.md).
217	- [Native mirroring across clusters](20260720-native-mirroring.md).

# Projects define the primary processing cell

Status: Accepted; partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).
Date: 2026-09-09

Implementation and rollout: [Projects define primary processing cell and placement rules](https://linear.app/entirehq/project/projects-define-primary-processing-cell-and-placement-rules-bd55ec1c3cb9/overview).

## TLDR

Each project defines one primary processing cell. Its repo groups inherit that
cell for authoritative non-Git data and the processing of that data. Git replicas
can exist in other cells. Git-data primaries remain a separate concept.

Native projects and GitHub mirrors projects remain separate. This decision does
not combine their permission models.

## Context

A repo group currently selects a processing-primary placement independently of
its project. That placement identifies the cell that stores the group's
authoritative non-Git application data, including trails, repo activity, and
search indices. Processing of that data runs in the same cell. The Git-data
primary separately identifies the canonical source of the repo's Git data.

Project-level features, such as trails, need access to data from their repos.
Projects and their repos can currently resolve to different cells. Application
cells cannot read another cell's private data to assemble those features.

Projects store a jurisdiction in `Project.Region`, but not an explicit processing
cell. ProjectDirectory derives a cluster slug only when exactly one serving
cluster matches that jurisdiction. A jurisdiction is not a cell. Adding a cluster
must not change the home of existing project data.

GitHub mirror creation already uses one system-managed project per upstream
owner, across all cells. Its existing region reflects the request that first
created the project. That value is not evidence of an intentional processing home.

## Decision

### The project owns processing placement

A project has one explicit primary processing cell, recorded by the control
plane. The cell must satisfy the project's jurisdiction and residency rules.
The assignment exists independently of repo membership, including for an empty
project.

The project's authoritative non-Git data lives in this cell. Each owned repo
group's authoritative non-Git data lives there too. Work that produces or changes
that authoritative state runs there. This includes project trails, repo activity,
and authoritative search indices.

The owning project is the only placement authority for a repo group. A reference
from another project does not confer ownership or change placement.

### Repo groups select a local processing placement

A group's processing-primary placement must belong to its project's processing
cell. It identifies the local placement that performs the group's work; it does
not define an independent processing home.

Each repo group needs a usable Git placement in that cell. Creation, adoption,
reconciliation, and admin overrides must preserve this rule. Replica creation in
another cell must not reassign the group or change its processing home.

The assigned cell and processing availability are separate states. When no local
placement can process a repo, the assignment remains unchanged. The system reports
processing as unavailable or pending. It does not elect a placement in another
cell merely because that placement has a healthy Git copy.

Project-only operations do not depend on the health or existence of a particular
repo placement. Replica maintenance can still run in each replica's own cell.

### Git-data primaries remain separate

| Concept | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| Primary processing cell | Project |
| Processing-primary placement for the group | Repo group |
| Canonical Git source | Repo group's Git-data primary |

For GitHub mirrors, GitHub remains the Git-data primary. A mirror in the project's
cell supplies local Git data for processing. Other mirrors remain valid placements.

New native repos start in their project's processing cell. Their initial Git-data
primary is therefore local, but Git authority and processing authority remain
distinct. This decision does not promote an existing native replica or change an
existing native Git-data primary. Native-primary promotion requires its own safe
handover, as described in the [native mirroring ADR](20260720-native-mirroring.md).

### Project kinds and permissions stay separate

Native projects contain native repo groups. GitHub mirrors projects contain
GitHub repo groups. Placement inheritance applies to both kinds without combining
their permission models.

Under this decision, each owner-scoped mirrors project has one processing cell
for all its repo groups. Additional Git placements do not create additional
project owners.

This decision grants no new access. GitHub-derived repo permissions remain in
force. Permission to create a mirror does not grant permission to relocate its
project. Authorization for project-level features remains a separate contract;
co-location alone never authorizes access to another repo's data.

### Assignment changes require migration

A project cell change is a data migration, not an ordinary metadata edit.
Reassigning a repo group to a project in another cell also requires migration.
The initial implementation does not provide general-purpose transfer or automatic
cross-cell failover.

Routing for authoritative non-Git operations follows the project assignment.
A fallback suitable for a Git read cannot select the destination for an
authoritative non-Git write. Unknown or unavailable placement must not cause a
write in an arbitrary cell.

Future non-Git replication can add copies outside the primary cell. Replication
does not itself grant write authority. A future promotion or multi-writer protocol
must define data readiness, conflict handling, and protection against stale writers.

## Future extension: project placement policy

The project can later define a broader placement policy for its repo groups.
This can cover primary placement and the regions or cells available for
additional placements:

- The primary processing cell.
- The placement of native Git-data primaries, independently of processing primaries.
- The regions and cells in which Git replicas or future non-Git replicas are permitted.

GitHub remains the canonical Git source for GitHub mirrors. Project policy governs
Entire placements; it does not relocate an external forge's Git-data primary.

An available location permits placement; it does not require a replica there.
Policy must respect residency constraints. Changing policy does not itself move
data or promote a primary. Existing placements need an explicit reconciliation
and migration path when they no longer satisfy the policy.

This is an extension point, not part of the initial implementation. The current
decision establishes project-owned processing placement without adding a general
placement-policy system.

## Migration and compatibility

The invariant is independent of the existing placement inventory. A read-only
analysis informs rollout; it does not gate this architectural decision.

Existing mirrors projects can have disjoint placement sets. One repo might exist
only in US and another only in EU. Migration must choose an explicit destination
and add any missing Git placements there. Existing replicas can remain.

> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
> New mirrors projects use US regardless of owner residency. Existing projects still require explicit migration decisions.

A cell with a complete Git placement set is a useful candidate, not necessarily
the owner's preferred destination. US is not a mandatory home. Destination
selection must respect residency requirements and account for the lack of a
self-service transfer operation. The existing race-selected region is not a
sufficient basis for that choice.

A complete Git placement set does not imply complete non-Git state. A fresh clone
cannot recover trails or other authoritative application records. Migration must
locate that state, transfer it safely, and verify it before activating the new
home. Derived data can be rebuilt only where its source is complete.

A primary-pointer update and a best-effort announcement do not constitute a safe
handover. Cutover must prevent old workers and writers from continuing against the
previous home. Migration must use an authorized transfer mechanism without relaxing
normal cell isolation. Source deletion follows verification and the recovery policy.

Deploy compatible schema and consumers before enforcing the assignment. Track
legacy projects explicitly during rollout. Features that require project-wide
locality remain disabled until the project and its repo groups satisfy the rule.
Changes in cluster topology must not silently relocate a project.

A code rollback must preserve the assignment and the active data home. Code that
can elect an out-of-cell primary is not safe after cutover. Operators must retain
a verified recovery path rather than treat a schema rollback as data recovery.

## Consequences

- Project-level features can access owned repo data within one cell.
- A project becomes a unit of processing placement and correlated availability.
- Large mirrors projects concentrate authoritative processing in one cell.
- Missing home placements add Git storage and replication traffic.
- Git replicas elsewhere do not provide non-Git failover by themselves.
- Cross-project references do not solve cross-cell reads or authorization.
- Placement remains explicit as additional cells and replication modes appear.

## Alternatives considered

**Use the project cell only as a default.** Rejected. Repo overrides and automatic
re-election would recreate the locality mismatch.

**Resolve the cell from jurisdiction on each request.** Rejected. A jurisdiction
can contain multiple cells. Infrastructure changes must not redefine data ownership.

**Allow cross-cell reads for project features.** Rejected for this design. That
would weaken cell independence and introduce a distributed dependency for local work.

> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
> US is mandatory for new mirrors projects. This does not relocate existing projects or constrain additional Git placements.

**Put every GitHub mirror in US permanently.** Not selected. US can be a migration
candidate where permitted, but it is not an architectural requirement.

## Delivery

The [Linear project](https://linear.app/entirehq/project/projects-define-primary-processing-cell-and-placement-rules-bd55ec1c3cb9/overview)
tracks implementation slices, consumer coordination, migration analysis, destination
selection, transfer tooling, verification, and rollout. This ADR records the
invariant and compatibility requirements, not the execution plan.

Related decisions:

- [Every repo belongs to a repo group](20260715-repo-group-for-every-repo.md).
- [Native mirroring across clusters](20260720-native-mirroring.md).

1	# Make entire-core responsible for native-mirror target eligibility
2	
3	- Status: Proposed
4	- Date: 2026-09-26
5	- Issue: COR-1977
6	- Consumers: ENT-2537 (existing repository), ENT-2538 (repository creation)
7	- Related: [20260909-project-primary-processing-cell](20260909-project-primary-processing-cell.md),
8	  [20260724-rsl-root-of-trust-mvp](20260724-rsl-root-of-trust-mvp.md)
9	
10	## Context
11	
12	The console and its BFF decide which native-mirror targets to offer. They
13	reconstruct backend rules from topology and repository placement data.
14	entire-core checks those rules again when the user creates a mirror.
15	
16	This gives the frontend responsibility for policy that the backend owns.
17	A change to placement policy requires coordinated changes across repositories.
18	Consumers can disagree with creation when they omit a check or interpret
19	missing capability data differently.
20	
21	The duplicated logic lives in the `entire.io` repository:
22	
23	- `projectRepositoryCellTargets` and `createProjectRepositoryRegions` filter
24	  creation choices in `projectRepositoryRegions.ts`.
25	- `loadNativeRepoDataResidency` computes `canAdd` in `repo-data-residency.ts`.
26	- `repositoryRegions.ts` filters occupied targets and applies a jurisdiction
27	  fallback when `canAdd` is absent.
28	
29	Core owns the cluster registry, placement records, authorization checks, and
30	creation admission setting. The admission setting belongs to the primary's
31	jurisdiction, which can differ from the caller's home jurisdiction.
32	Publishing more topology fields would still require each consumer to combine
33	these facts into its own eligibility rule.
34	
35	## Decision
36	
37	entire-core computes native-mirror target eligibility. The frontend requests
38	eligible targets and presents them to the user. The BFF handles authenticated
39	routing without reconstructing placement policy.
40	
41	Core provides two endpoints:
42	
43	```text
44	GET /api/v1/repos/{repoId}/available-placements
45	GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/available-placements
46	```
47	
48	The repository endpoint uses the repository's primary placement. The project
49	endpoint uses the placement that repository creation resolves from the
50	project's assigned processing cell.
51	
52	The listings and `CreateNativeMirror` share the per-target predicate,
53	`admitNativeMirrorTarget`. New per-target rules belong in that predicate.
54	A target must be live, visible, capable of hosting native mirrors, and outside
55	the primary's cluster and jurisdiction.
56	
57	Discovery and creation also share project authorization, primary eligibility,
58	and creation admission checks. These checks use loaded facts. Discovery reuses
59	the repository and placement loaded during authorization; creation retains its
60	fresh reads before mutation.
61	
62	The repository listing also excludes every cluster in a cell with an existing
63	placement in the repository group. Retry of a failed placement remains a separate action
64	on the placement status surface.
65	
66	`GET /api/v1/topology` continues to provide topology and display labels.
67	Consumers use it to label returned targets, without applying additional
68	capability or jurisdiction rules.
69	
70	### Authorization and jurisdiction
71	
72	The repository endpoint requires `manage` authority on the native primary.
73	The project endpoint requires `create_repo` permission. It also applies
74	repository creation's restrictions for forge-managed projects and organization
75	SSO sessions.
76	
77	Both endpoints resolve the subject's jurisdiction before checking creation
78	admission. A request to another jurisdiction receives `421`. The consumer must
79	route or retry the request against the authoritative Core.
80	
81	The endpoints register on the customer API under `NativeMirrorEnabled()`.
82	They do not register on the admin API, which uses different authority rules.
83	
84	### Response and failures
85	
86	Each target identifies a cluster and its position in the topology:
87	
88	```json
89	{
90	  "targets": [
91	    {
92	      "clusterSlug": "purina",
93	      "jurisdiction": "us",
94	      "cell": "aws-us-east-2"
95	    }
96	  ]
97	}
98	```
99	
100	`clusterSlug` is the identifier accepted by mirror creation. `jurisdiction`
101	and `cell` identify the topology entries that provide display labels.
102	
103	An empty `200` response means no target passed the eligibility and occupancy
104	checks. Registry or occupancy read failures and undecidable authorization
105	checks return `503`. Paused creation or missing native-mirror configuration
106	also returns `503`.
107	
108	A project without an assigned processing cell receives `503`. Its legacy
109	creation path can select the responding Core's default cluster. The listing
110	does not use that path to infer the intended primary jurisdiction.
111	
112	### Limits of eligibility
113	
114	A listed target is a candidate, not a guarantee that creation succeeds.
115	Creation rechecks authorization, configuration, placement, and lifecycle state.
116	
117	The repository listing rejects inactive primaries with `409`.
118	The listings do not probe the data plane for trust capabilities or acquire
119	creation's group locks. Those checks remain on the mutation path.
120	Consumers must handle creation failures even after selecting a listed target.
121	
122	The repository listing resolves occupied cells from the same registry read
123	used for eligibility. Hidden and decommissioned clusters still contribute
124	occupied cells. Failed and deleting placements remain occupied until their
125	intent rows are removed. An occupied cluster with an unknown cell causes
126	`503`; Core cannot safely offer other clusters without that information.
127	
128	This preserves the BFF's cell-level exclusion without extra registry reads.
129	Creation checks cell occupancy inside the transaction that holds the group
130	lock. A different cluster in an occupied cell receives `409`. Unknown cell
131	data receives `503`. Concurrent additions cannot both claim the same cell.
132	Same-cluster requests retain existing idempotency and retry behavior. Existing
133	placements remain retryable even when a legacy group already shares a cell.
134	
135	Each refusal carries an RFC 9457 problem type, because the statuses mix
136	lasting and passing conditions:
137	
138	- `native-mirror/cell-occupied` (`409`): a live placement holds the cell.
139	  The refusal lasts until that placement is removed.
140	- `native-mirror/cell-vacating` (`409`): only placements marked for deletion
141	  hold the cell. A retry can succeed after teardown removes their rows.
142	- `native-mirror/cell-unknown` (`503`): the registry records no cell for a
143	  cluster involved. An operator must correct the registry.
144	
145	Asynchronous creation applies the same rule at three points:
146	
147	1. Repository creation rejects two requested clusters in one cell with `400`.
148	2. A queued request for a cell with a live placement receives the
149	   `cell-occupied` `409` at submission. A vacating cell is accepted.
150	3. The request job fails an occupied cell with `region_unavailable`. It
151	   retries a vacating or unknown cell until the give-up age.
152	
153	### Reads and caching
154	
155	The repository listing reuses the placement loaded during authorization.
156	Neither listing makes data-plane calls. Registry enumeration remains uncached
157	in the cluster store.
158	
159	The repository response uses `private, no-cache` and an `ETag`. The project
160	response uses `private, max-age=30`. Both responses vary on `Authorization`
161	and `Cookie` to separate callers using either authentication method.
162	
163	Consumers fetch targets when the picker opens and invalidate them after
164	placement mutations. Placement status polling remains a separate query.
165	This keeps authorization and eligibility reads off the frequent status poll.
166	
167	## Alternatives considered
168	
169	**Publish capability flags on topology.** This exposes more inputs but leaves
170	consumers responsible for combining them with authorization, admission, and
171	placement rules. It does not resolve the ownership problem.
172	
173	**Return eligibility with residency status.** This can also centralize policy
174	in Core. Separate endpoints support both repository and project scopes and
175	let consumers fetch eligibility independently from status polling.
176	
177	**Keep eligibility in the BFF.** This removes some browser logic but still
178	duplicates Core's policy in another service. The BFF remains responsible for
179	transport and routing instead.
180	
181	## Delivery and compatibility
182	
183	Deliver Core and the consumer changes as one coordinated unit of work.
184	The APIs are additive and require no schema migration. Existing consumers
185	continue to work while Core rolls out. Direct callers can no longer add a
186	second cluster in an occupied cell. The console already excludes these choices.
187	Existing placements require no migration and remain readable and removable.
188	
189	Deploy the mutation guard to every writer before relying on this invariant.
190	Old writers can still accept conflicting additions during a mixed deployment.
191	Rolling Core back restores that gap but does not invalidate stored records.
192	The existing request telemetry exposes occupancy conflicts as `409` responses.
193	
194	1. Deploy the endpoints to every participating Core jurisdiction.
195	2. Verify routing for callers whose home differs from the subject's jurisdiction.
196	3. Enable the consumer changes in `entire.io`.
197	
198	ENT-2538 replaces the creation picker's eligibility calculations with the
199	project endpoint. ENT-2537 replaces the BFF's `canAdd` computation and the
200	existing repository picker's fallback with the repository endpoint.
201	Consumers retain presentation, selection, and pending-request state.
202	
203	A consumer treats `404` or `503` as unavailable eligibility. It does not
204	silently reconstruct the removed rules. Projects awaiting processing-cell
205	assignment therefore cannot offer additional targets through this API.
206	
207	Roll back the consumer before removing Core support for these endpoints.
208	Disabling `ENTIRE_NATIVE_MIRROR_ENABLED` also disables existing native-mirror
209	operations, so it is not a rollback mechanism for the picker alone.
210	
211	## Consequences and verification
212	
213	Core owns eligibility policy across creation and discovery. Consumers no
214	longer need to track changes to that policy. The listings add authorized
215	backend reads beyond the existing topology request.
216	
217	Core tests cover the shared predicate, authorization, jurisdiction routing,
218	occupancy, unavailable dependencies, and cache behavior. Contract tests verify
219	that returned target identities join to topology entries, including shipped
220	fixtures.
221	
222	Consumer verification must cover both picker flows, foreign jurisdictions,
223	empty and unavailable responses, and creation failures after selection.
224	It must also cover projects without an assigned processing cell and cells
225	that contain multiple clusters.

1	# Projects define the primary processing cell
2	
3	Status: Accepted; partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).
4	Date: 2026-09-09
5	
6	Implementation and rollout: [Projects define primary processing cell and placement rules](https://linear.app/entirehq/project/projects-define-primary-processing-cell-and-placement-rules-bd55ec1c3cb9/overview).
7	
8	## TLDR
9	
10	Each project defines one primary processing cell. Its repo groups inherit that
11	cell for authoritative non-Git data and the processing of that data. Git replicas
12	can exist in other cells. Git-data primaries remain a separate concept.
13	
14	Native projects and GitHub mirrors projects remain separate. This decision does
15	not combine their permission models.
16	
17	## Context
18	
19	A repo group currently selects a processing-primary placement independently of
20	its project. That placement identifies the cell that stores the group's
21	authoritative non-Git application data, including trails, repo activity, and
22	search indices. Processing of that data runs in the same cell. The Git-data
23	primary separately identifies the canonical source of the repo's Git data.
24	
25	Project-level features, such as trails, need access to data from their repos.
26	Projects and their repos can currently resolve to different cells. Application
27	cells cannot read another cell's private data to assemble those features.
28	
29	Projects store a jurisdiction in `Project.Region`, but not an explicit processing
30	cell. ProjectDirectory derives a cluster slug only when exactly one serving
31	cluster matches that jurisdiction. A jurisdiction is not a cell. Adding a cluster
32	must not change the home of existing project data.
33	
34	GitHub mirror creation already uses one system-managed project per upstream
35	owner, across all cells. Its existing region reflects the request that first
36	created the project. That value is not evidence of an intentional processing home.
37	
38	## Decision
39	
40	### The project owns processing placement
41	
42	A project has one explicit primary processing cell, recorded by the control
43	plane. The cell must satisfy the project's jurisdiction and residency rules.
44	The assignment exists independently of repo membership, including for an empty
45	project.
46	
47	The project's authoritative non-Git data lives in this cell. Each owned repo
48	group's authoritative non-Git data lives there too. Work that produces or changes
49	that authoritative state runs there. This includes project trails, repo activity,
50	and authoritative search indices.
51	
52	The owning project is the only placement authority for a repo group. A reference
53	from another project does not confer ownership or change placement.
54	
55	### Repo groups select a local processing placement
56	
57	A group's processing-primary placement must belong to its project's processing
58	cell. It identifies the local placement that performs the group's work; it does
59	not define an independent processing home.
60	
61	Each repo group needs a usable Git placement in that cell. Creation, adoption,
62	reconciliation, and admin overrides must preserve this rule. Replica creation in
63	another cell must not reassign the group or change its processing home.
64	
65	The assigned cell and processing availability are separate states. When no local
66	placement can process a repo, the assignment remains unchanged. The system reports
67	processing as unavailable or pending. It does not elect a placement in another
68	cell merely because that placement has a healthy Git copy.
69	
70	Project-only operations do not depend on the health or existence of a particular
71	repo placement. Replica maintenance can still run in each replica's own cell.
72	
73	### Git-data primaries remain separate
74	
75	| Concept | Authority |
76	| --- | --- |
77	| Primary processing cell | Project |
78	| Processing-primary placement for the group | Repo group |
79	| Canonical Git source | Repo group's Git-data primary |
80	
81	For GitHub mirrors, GitHub remains the Git-data primary. A mirror in the project's
82	cell supplies local Git data for processing. Other mirrors remain valid placements.
83	
84	New native repos start in their project's processing cell. Their initial Git-data
85	primary is therefore local, but Git authority and processing authority remain
86	distinct. This decision does not promote an existing native replica or change an
87	existing native Git-data primary. Native-primary promotion requires its own safe
88	handover, as described in the [native mirroring ADR](20260720-native-mirroring.md).
89	
90	### Project kinds and permissions stay separate
91	
92	Native projects contain native repo groups. GitHub mirrors projects contain
93	GitHub repo groups. Placement inheritance applies to both kinds without combining
94	their permission models.
95	
96	Under this decision, each owner-scoped mirrors project has one processing cell
97	for all its repo groups. Additional Git placements do not create additional
98	project owners.
99	
100	This decision grants no new access. GitHub-derived repo permissions remain in
101	force. Permission to create a mirror does not grant permission to relocate its
102	project. Authorization for project-level features remains a separate contract;
103	co-location alone never authorizes access to another repo's data.
104	
105	### Assignment changes require migration
106	
107	A project cell change is a data migration, not an ordinary metadata edit.
108	Reassigning a repo group to a project in another cell also requires migration.
109	The initial implementation does not provide general-purpose transfer or automatic
110	cross-cell failover.
111	
112	Routing for authoritative non-Git operations follows the project assignment.
113	A fallback suitable for a Git read cannot select the destination for an
114	authoritative non-Git write. Unknown or unavailable placement must not cause a
115	write in an arbitrary cell.
116	
117	Future non-Git replication can add copies outside the primary cell. Replication
118	does not itself grant write authority. A future promotion or multi-writer protocol
119	must define data readiness, conflict handling, and protection against stale writers.
120	
121	## Future extension: project placement policy
122	
123	The project can later define a broader placement policy for its repo groups.
124	This can cover primary placement and the regions or cells available for
125	additional placements:
126	
127	- The primary processing cell.
128	- The placement of native Git-data primaries, independently of processing primaries.
129	- The regions and cells in which Git replicas or future non-Git replicas are permitted.
130	
131	GitHub remains the canonical Git source for GitHub mirrors. Project policy governs
132	Entire placements; it does not relocate an external forge's Git-data primary.
133	
134	An available location permits placement; it does not require a replica there.
135	Policy must respect residency constraints. Changing policy does not itself move
136	data or promote a primary. Existing placements need an explicit reconciliation
137	and migration path when they no longer satisfy the policy.
138	
139	This is an extension point, not part of the initial implementation. The current
140	decision establishes project-owned processing placement without adding a general
141	placement-policy system.
142	
143	## Migration and compatibility
144	
145	The invariant is independent of the existing placement inventory. A read-only
146	analysis informs rollout; it does not gate this architectural decision.
147	
148	Existing mirrors projects can have disjoint placement sets. One repo might exist
149	only in US and another only in EU. Migration must choose an explicit destination
150	and add any missing Git placements there. Existing replicas can remain.
151	
152	> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
153	> New mirrors projects use US regardless of owner residency. Existing projects still require explicit migration decisions.
154	
155	A cell with a complete Git placement set is a useful candidate, not necessarily
156	the owner's preferred destination. US is not a mandatory home. Destination
157	selection must respect residency requirements and account for the lack of a
158	self-service transfer operation. The existing race-selected region is not a
159	sufficient basis for that choice.
160	
161	A complete Git placement set does not imply complete non-Git state. A fresh clone
162	cannot recover trails or other authoritative application records. Migration must
163	locate that state, transfer it safely, and verify it before activating the new
164	home. Derived data can be rebuilt only where its source is complete.
165	
166	A primary-pointer update and a best-effort announcement do not constitute a safe
167	handover. Cutover must prevent old workers and writers from continuing against the
168	previous home. Migration must use an authorized transfer mechanism without relaxing
169	normal cell isolation. Source deletion follows verification and the recovery policy.
170	
171	Deploy compatible schema and consumers before enforcing the assignment. Track
172	legacy projects explicitly during rollout. Features that require project-wide
173	locality remain disabled until the project and its repo groups satisfy the rule.
174	Changes in cluster topology must not silently relocate a project.
175	
176	A code rollback must preserve the assignment and the active data home. Code that
177	can elect an out-of-cell primary is not safe after cutover. Operators must retain
178	a verified recovery path rather than treat a schema rollback as data recovery.
179	
180	## Consequences
181	
182	- Project-level features can access owned repo data within one cell.
183	- A project becomes a unit of processing placement and correlated availability.
184	- Large mirrors projects concentrate authoritative processing in one cell.
185	- Missing home placements add Git storage and replication traffic.
186	- Git replicas elsewhere do not provide non-Git failover by themselves.
187	- Cross-project references do not solve cross-cell reads or authorization.
188	- Placement remains explicit as additional cells and replication modes appear.
189	
190	## Alternatives considered
191	
192	**Use the project cell only as a default.** Rejected. Repo overrides and automatic
193	re-election would recreate the locality mismatch.
194	
195	**Resolve the cell from jurisdiction on each request.** Rejected. A jurisdiction
196	can contain multiple cells. Infrastructure changes must not redefine data ownership.
197	
198	**Allow cross-cell reads for project features.** Rejected for this design. That
199	would weaken cell independence and introduce a distributed dependency for local work.
200	
201	> **Partially superseded by [New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home](20260915-new-mirrors-projects-us-home.md).**
202	> US is mandatory for new mirrors projects. This does not relocate existing projects or constrain additional Git placements.
203	
204	**Put every GitHub mirror in US permanently.** Not selected. US can be a migration
205	candidate where permitted, but it is not an architectural requirement.
206	
207	## Delivery
208	
209	The [Linear project](https://linear.app/entirehq/project/projects-define-primary-processing-cell-and-placement-rules-bd55ec1c3cb9/overview)
210	tracks implementation slices, consumer coordination, migration analysis, destination
211	selection, transfer tooling, verification, and rollout. This ADR records the
212	invariant and compatibility requirements, not the execution plan.
213	
214	Related decisions:
215	
216	- [Every repo belongs to a repo group](20260715-repo-group-for-every-repo.md).
217	- [Native mirroring across clusters](20260720-native-mirroring.md).
218

1	# New GitHub mirrors projects use a US home
2	
3	Status: Accepted
4	Date: 2026-09-15
5	Supersedes: [Projects define the primary processing cell](20260909-project-primary-processing-cell.md), only its non-mandatory-US policy for new mirrors projects.
6	
7	## Decision
8	
9	The earlier ADR says US is not a mandatory home for GitHub mirrors projects.
10	New mirrors projects now select US regardless of owner residency or the requesting core's jurisdiction.
11	Mirror work reads from GitHub, so platform policy selects US.
12	
13	Both the region and processing cell seeds derive from this policy.
14	The region seed is unconditional; `ENTIRE_PROJECT_CELL_ASSIGNMENT_ENABLED` still gates the cell assignment.
15	
16	Existing projects retain their stored home; COR-1546 owns migration.
17	This decision does not change native repo placement, mirror processing-primary election, or permissions.
18	The earlier ADR's remaining placement and migration requirements still apply.
19	
20	See the [rollout runbook](../runbooks/mirrors-project-us-home.md) for consumer compatibility and the divergence inventory.

1	# Make entire-core responsible for native-mirror target eligibility
2	
3	- Status: Proposed
4	- Date: 2026-09-26
5	- Issue: COR-1977
6	- Consumers: ENT-2537 (existing repository), ENT-2538 (repository creation)
7	- Related: [20260909-project-primary-processing-cell](20260909-project-primary-processing-cell.md),
8	  [20260724-rsl-root-of-trust-mvp](20260724-rsl-root-of-trust-mvp.md)
9	
10	## Context
11	
12	The console and its BFF decide which native-mirror targets to offer. They
13	reconstruct backend rules from topology and repository placement data.
14	entire-core checks those rules again when the user creates a mirror.
15	
16	This gives the frontend responsibility for policy that the backend owns.
17	A change to placement policy requires coordinated changes across repositories.
18	Consumers can disagree with creation when they omit a check or interpret
19	missing capability data differently.
20	
21	The duplicated logic lives in the `entire.io` repository:
22	
23	- `projectRepositoryCellTargets` and `createProjectRepositoryRegions` filter
24	  creation choices in `projectRepositoryRegions.ts`.
25	- `loadNativeRepoDataResidency` computes `canAdd` in `repo-data-residency.ts`.
26	- `repositoryRegions.ts` filters occupied targets and applies a jurisdiction
27	  fallback when `canAdd` is absent.
28	
29	Core owns the cluster registry, placement records, authorization checks, and
30	creation admission setting. The admission setting belongs to the primary's
31	jurisdiction, which can differ from the caller's home jurisdiction.
32	Publishing more topology fields would still require each consumer to combine
33	these facts into its own eligibility rule.
34	
35	## Decision
36	
37	entire-core computes native-mirror target eligibility. The frontend requests
38	eligible targets and presents them to the user. The BFF handles authenticated
39	routing without reconstructing placement policy.
40	
41	Core provides two endpoints:
42	
43	```text
44	GET /api/v1/repos/{repoId}/available-placements
45	GET /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/available-placements
46	```
47	
48	The repository endpoint uses the repository's primary placement. The project
49	endpoint uses the placement that repository creation resolves from the
50	project's assigned processing cell.
51	
52	The listings and `CreateNativeMirror` share the per-target predicate,
53	`admitNativeMirrorTarget`. New per-target rules belong in that predicate.
54	A target must be live, visible, capable of hosting native mirrors, and outside
55	the primary's cluster and jurisdiction.
56	
57	Discovery and creation also share project authorization, primary eligibility,
58	and creation admission checks. These checks use loaded facts. Discovery reuses
59	the repository and placement loaded during authorization; creation retains its
60	fresh reads before mutation.
61	
62	The repository listing also excludes every cluster in a cell with an existing
63	placement in the repository group. Retry of a failed placement remains a separate action
64	on the placement status surface.
65	
66	`GET /api/v1/topology` continues to provide topology and display labels.
67	Consumers use it to label returned targets, without applying additional
68	capability or jurisdiction rules.
69	
70	### Authorization and jurisdiction
71	
72	The repository endpoint requires `manage` authority on the native primary.
73	The project endpoint requires `create_repo` permission. It also applies
74	repository creation's restrictions for forge-managed projects and organization
75	SSO sessions.
76	
77	Both endpoints resolve the subject's jurisdiction before checking creation
78	admission. A request to another jurisdiction receives `421`. The consumer must
79	route or retry the request against the authoritative Core.
80	
81	The endpoints register on the customer API under `NativeMirrorEnabled()`.
82	They do not register on the admin API, which uses different authority rules.
83	
84	### Response and failures
85	
86	Each target identifies a cluster and its position in the topology:
87	
88	```json
89	{
90	  "targets": [
91	    {
92	      "clusterSlug": "purina",
93	      "jurisdiction": "us",
94	      "cell": "aws-us-east-2"
95	    }
96	  ]
97	}
98	```
99	
100	`clusterSlug` is the identifier accepted by mirror creation. `jurisdiction`
101	and `cell` identify the topology entries that provide display labels.
102	
103	An empty `200` response means no target passed the eligibility and occupancy
104	checks. Registry or occupancy read failures and undecidable authorization
105	checks return `503`. Paused creation or missing native-mirror configuration
106	also returns `503`.
107	
108	A project without an assigned processing cell receives `503`. Its legacy
109	creation path can select the responding Core's default cluster. The listing
110	does not use that path to infer the intended primary jurisdiction.
111	
112	### Limits of eligibility
113	
114	A listed target is a candidate, not a guarantee that creation succeeds.
115	Creation rechecks authorization, configuration, placement, and lifecycle state.
116	
117	The repository listing rejects inactive primaries with `409`.
118	The listings do not probe the data plane for trust capabilities or acquire
119	creation's group locks. Those checks remain on the mutation path.
120	Consumers must handle creation failures even after selecting a listed target.
121	
122	The repository listing resolves occupied cells from the same registry read
123	used for eligibility. Hidden and decommissioned clusters still contribute
124	occupied cells. Failed and deleting placements remain occupied until their
125	intent rows are removed. An occupied cluster with an unknown cell causes
126	`503`; Core cannot safely offer other clusters without that information.
127	
128	This preserves the BFF's cell-level exclusion without extra registry reads.
129	Creation checks cell occupancy inside the transaction that holds the group
130	lock. A different cluster in an occupied cell receives `409`. Unknown cell
131	data receives `503`. Concurrent additions cannot both claim the same cell.
132	Same-cluster requests retain existing idempotency and retry behavior. Existing
133	placements remain retryable even when a legacy group already shares a cell.
134	
135	Each refusal carries an RFC 9457 problem type, because the statuses mix
136	lasting and passing conditions:
137	
138	- `native-mirror/cell-occupied` (`409`): a live placement holds the cell.
139	  The refusal lasts until that placement is removed.
140	- `native-mirror/cell-vacating` (`409`): only placements marked for deletion
141	  hold the cell. A retry can succeed after teardown removes their rows.
142	- `native-mirror/cell-unknown` (`503`): the registry records no cell for a
143	  cluster involved. An operator must correct the registry.
144	
145	Asynchronous creation applies the same rule at three points:
146	
147	1. Repository creation rejects two requested clusters in one cell with `400`.
148	2. A queued request for a cell with a live placement receives the
149	   `cell-occupied` `409` at submission. A vacating cell is accepted.
150	3. The request job fails an occupied cell with `region_unavailable`. It
151	   retries a vacating or unknown cell until the give-up age.
152	
153	### Reads and caching
154	
155	The repository listing reuses the placement loaded during authorization.
156	Neither listing makes data-plane calls. Registry enumeration remains uncached
157	in the cluster store.
158	
159	The repository response uses `private, no-cache` and an `ETag`. The project
160	response uses `private, max-age=30`. Both responses vary on `Authorization`
161	and `Cookie` to separate callers using either authentication method.
162	
163	Consumers fetch targets when the picker opens and invalidate them after
164	placement mutations. Placement status polling remains a separate query.
165	This keeps authorization and eligibility reads off the frequent status poll.
166	
167	## Alternatives considered
168	
169	**Publish capability flags on topology.** This exposes more inputs but leaves
170	consumers responsible for combining them with authorization, admission, and
171	placement rules. It does not resolve the ownership problem.
172	
173	**Return eligibility with residency status.** This can also centralize policy
174	in Core. Separate endpoints support both repository and project scopes and
175	let consumers fetch eligibility independently from status polling.
176	
177	**Keep eligibility in the BFF.** This removes some browser logic but still
178	duplicates Core's policy in another service. The BFF remains responsible for
179	transport and routing instead.
180	
181	## Delivery and compatibility
182	
183	Deliver Core and the consumer changes as one coordinated unit of work.
184	The APIs are additive and require no schema migration. Existing consumers
185	continue to work while Core rolls out. Direct callers can no longer add a
186	second cluster in an occupied cell. The console already excludes these choices.
187	Existing placements require no migration and remain readable and removable.
188	
189	Deploy the mutation guard to every writer before relying on this invariant.
190	Old writers can still accept conflicting additions during a mixed deployment.
191	Rolling Core back restores that gap but does not invalidate stored records.
192	The existing request telemetry exposes occupancy conflicts as `409` responses.
193	
194	1. Deploy the endpoints to every participating Core jurisdiction.
195	2. Verify routing for callers whose home differs from the subject's jurisdiction.
196	3. Enable the consumer changes in `entire.io`.
197	
198	ENT-2538 replaces the creation picker's eligibility calculations with the
199	project endpoint. ENT-2537 replaces the BFF's `canAdd` computation and the
200	existing repository picker's fallback with the repository endpoint.
201	Consumers retain presentation, selection, and pending-request state.
202	
203	A consumer treats `404` or `503` as unavailable eligibility. It does not
204	silently reconstruct the removed rules. Projects awaiting processing-cell
205	assignment therefore cannot offer additional targets through this API.
206	
207	Roll back the consumer before removing Core support for these endpoints.
208	Disabling `ENTIRE_NATIVE_MIRROR_ENABLED` also disables existing native-mirror
209	operations, so it is not a rollback mechanism for the picker alone.
210	
211	## Consequences and verification
212	
213	Core owns eligibility policy across creation and discovery. Consumers no
214	longer need to track changes to that policy. The listings add authorized
215	backend reads beyond the existing topology request.
216	
217	Core tests cover the shared predicate, authorization, jurisdiction routing,
218	occupancy, unavailable dependencies, and cache behavior. Contract tests verify
219	that returned target identities join to topology entries, including shipped
220	fixtures.
221	
222	Consumer verification must cover both picker flows, foreign jurisdictions,
223	empty and unavailable responses, and creation failures after selection.
224	It must also cover projects without an assigned processing cell and cells
225	that contain multiple clusters.
226

1:// RepoLookup is the internal cross-jurisdictional directory: given upstream
2:// mirror coordinates, returns every (jurisdiction, cluster_slug) that
3:// mirrors them. Used by webhook ingest to fan a single upstream event out
4:// across the per-cluster NATS subjects defined by ADR 20260408.
6:// Auth: mTLS-only. The receiver listener gates by per-listener workload
7:// allowlist (ADR 20260501); there is no end-user identity in these calls.
15:service RepoLookup {
16:  // LookupByMirror resolves upstream mirror coordinates to every routable
17:  // placement that hosts a mirror of them. An upstream may be mirrored in
18:  // multiple jurisdictions/clusters; the response carries the full list,
19:  // ordered by (jurisdiction, cluster_slug).
20:  //
21:  // Placements without a cluster_slug (legacy rows still in the COR-138
22:  // backfill window) are filtered server-side and logged at warn level —
23:  // they are not addressable on per-cluster NATS subjects, so returning
24:  // them would silently route work nowhere. An empty response means no
25:  // routable mirror exists; it does not distinguish "no mirror at all"
26:  // from "all mirrors are still unstamped."
27:  rpc LookupByMirror(LookupByMirrorRequest) returns (LookupByMirrorResponse);
29:  // LookupMirrorByID is LookupByMirror's inverse: given a mirror's EntireDB
30:  // repo ULID, return the upstream coordinates (provider/owner/repo) it
31:  // mirrors. Callers that hold only the mirror_repos id — e.g. a consumer of a
32:  // resource_lifecycle_v1 mirror.created event, whose payload is a thin
33:  // resource_id-only projection — use it to recover the (owner, repo) they
34:  // need to act on the mirror (COR-717: seed github_repo_meta on mirror
35:  // creation). Returns CodeNotFound when no mirror_repos row matches the id (or
36:  // the placement is suspended); CodeInvalidArgument when repo_id is empty or
37:  // not a valid ULID.
38:  rpc LookupMirrorByID(LookupMirrorByIDRequest) returns (LookupMirrorByIDResponse);
40:  // LookupNativeMirrorsByRepoID resolves a repo id (any placement of a native
41:  // repo — primary or native mirror; the id a repo_refs_v1 ref event carries) to
42:  // its group's git-data HOME placement and every REPLICATION-eligible
43:  // native-mirror placement (ADR 20260720-native-mirroring). Replica fan-out
44:  // consumes this: it drops the event unless its local cluster is the home
45:  // (loop prevention), then publishes one sync job per native mirror.
46:  // source_url is the home cluster's INTERNAL by-ID git URL, computed here so
47:  // fanout and the worker stay source-agnostic; it is never user-facing.
48:  //
49:  // Native mirrors below the serving stage (still being created), suspended, or
50:  // marked for deletion are excluded. Placements that ARE listed may still hold
51:  // an empty or partially-synced repo — a placement is listed from the moment
52:  // it is registered, and that replication traffic is what makes it converge,
53:  // so this response is not a statement that a mirror can serve READS. Read
54:  // routing gates separately, on the placement having converged; do not reuse
55:  // this RPC to answer "where may I read this repo from". An ungrouped repo
56:  // resolves to home = its own placement with no mirrors of either kind. A
57:  // GitHub mirror group resolves the same way unless one of its placements
58:  // owns the group's git data, in which case home is that owner and the
59:  // siblings come back as namespace_mirrors (see below); full-repo GitHub
60:  // mirroring still routes through LookupByMirror, not here. CodeNotFound
61:  // when the repo id is unknown; CodeInvalidArgument when it is empty or not
62:  // a ULID.

1	package main
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"errors"
6		"log/slog"
7		"slices"
8		"strings"
9		"time"
10	
11		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
12		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
13		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
14	
15		"github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/internal/mirrorjobs"
16		"github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/pkg/fanoutengine"
17		"github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/pkg/refevents"
18	)
19	
20	// Native-mirror trigger consumer (COR-1021): consumes the LOCAL cluster's
21	// repo_refs_v1 ref-event stream and publishes one mirror.git sync_repo job per
22	// serving native mirror of the pushed repo — the event-driven fast path that
23	// keeps native mirrors fresh. Enabled per cluster via
24	// FANOUT_NATIVE_MIRROR_CONSUMER_ENABLED; a no-op while no native mirrors exist
25	// (every event resolves to an empty route set and Acks).
26	const (
27		// nativeMirrorDurable is the pull-consumer durable on repo_refs_v1. A fixed
28		// name (unlike FANOUT_DURABLE) is safe here because the stream itself is
29		// per-cluster local — durables are stream-scoped, so two clusters' consumers
30		// can never collide on one stream the way the shared US webhook stream's
31		// could.
32		nativeMirrorDurable = "native-mirror-fanout"
33	
34		// Retry envelope: same flat-NakWithDelay shape as the webhook consumer.
35		// repo_refs_v1 is limits-retention, so an exhausted delivery is simply not
36		// redelivered again (nothing orphans, nothing pins). A dropped event is
37		// healed by the primary's next push — every sync replicates full ref
38		// state — so no DLQ is wired (rev 11: v1 accepts "next push" as the
39		// staleness RPO). No InactiveThreshold either: an abandoned durable on a
40		// limits stream pins nothing.
41		nativeMirrorFailureDelay = 30 * time.Second
42		nativeMirrorMaxDeliver   = 8
43		nativeMirrorAckWait      = 30 * time.Second
44	)
45	
46	// Ack reasons for benign no-op dispositions, recorded on the completed metric
47	// so drops are observable without per-event logs (not_home fires on every
48	// worker-push echo in a mirror cluster; no_native_mirrors on every push in a
49	// home cluster — both far too hot to log).
50	const (
51		ackReasonTlogRef      = "tlog_ref"          // transparency-log ref churn; the branch event triggers the sync
52		ackReasonRepoNotFound = "repo_not_found"    // repo deleted between event publish and consume
53		ackReasonNotHome      = "not_home"          // event echoed from a native-mirror placement (loop prevention)
54		ackReasonNoMirrors    = "no_native_mirrors" // repo has no serving native mirrors (every repo today)
55	
56		// ackReasonNamespaceOutOfScope fires on a namespace group (a GitHub
57		// group whose git data one placement owns): those placements replicate
58		// only the Entire-owned namespace from here, so every other ref —
59		// refs/heads/main, tags, HEAD symref moves — is acked without a job.
60		// Hot on the owner cell: one per ordinary push.
61		ackReasonNamespaceOutOfScope = "namespace_out_of_scope"
62	)
63	
64	// namespaceRefPrefix is the Entire-owned branch namespace replicated by
65	// entiredb_ns jobs (COR-1566). The worker enforces the same scope on the
66	// sync itself; this filter only keeps the jobs off the stream.
67	const namespaceRefPrefix = "refs/heads/entire/native/"
68	
69	// newNativeMirrorConsumer wires the ref-event resolver into the shared
70	// fanoutengine runtime. Same worker pool knobs and region map as the webhook
71	// consumer; no DLQ (see the retry-envelope comment above).
72	func newNativeMirrorConsumer(js nats.JetStreamContext, resolver *nativeMirrorSyncResolver, regions fanoutengine.Regions, metrics *fanoutMetrics, concurrency, fetchBatch int) *fanoutengine.Consumer {
73		return fanoutengine.New(js, refEventDecoder{}, resolver, regions, hooksFor(metrics), fanoutengine.Config{
74			Subject:         refevents.NATSSubjectPrefix + ">",
75			Stream:          refevents.NATSStreamName,
76			Durable:         nativeMirrorDurable,
77			Tracer:          tracerName,
78			SpanName:        "fanout.native_mirror.dispatch",
79			DestinationName: refevents.NATSStreamName,
80			AckWait:         nativeMirrorAckWait,
81			MaxDeliver:      nativeMirrorMaxDeliver,
82			NakDelay:        nativeMirrorFailureDelay,
83			SpanAttrs:       stampRefEventSpanAttrs,
84			Concurrency:     concurrency,
85			FetchBatch:      fetchBatch,
86		})
87	}
88	
89	// refEventDecoder turns a raw repo_refs_v1 delivery into the engine envelope.
90	// A decode failure → Term (bad envelope). Event carries the ref op so the
91	// completed metric's event attribute stays low-cardinality: the KNOWN wire
92	// vocabulary (create/update/delete/force_update/symref_update) passes
93	// through, anything else is clamped to "other" — Unmarshal tolerates
94	// newer-producer payloads by design, so the wire value is unbounded even
95	// though the payload is valid. DeliveryID is the producer's
96	// content+timestamp identity, which doubles as the engine's route-memo key.
97	type refEventDecoder struct{}
98	
99	// eventOther stands in for a ref op outside the known vocabulary on the
100	// metric attribute, so a future producer op can't create unbounded metric
101	// cardinality. Spans/logs still carry the real op via the resolver.
102	const eventOther = "other"
103	
104	var knownRefOps = map[string]bool{
105		refevents.RefOpCreate:       true,
106		refevents.RefOpUpdate:       true,
107		refevents.RefOpDelete:       true,
108		refevents.RefOpForceUpdate:  true,
109		refevents.RefOpSymrefUpdate: true,
110	}
111	
112	func (refEventDecoder) Decode(data []byte) (fanoutengine.Envelope, error) {
113		ev, err := refevents.Unmarshal(data)
114		if err != nil {
115			return fanoutengine.Envelope{}, err
116		}
117		event := ev.RefOp
118		if !knownRefOps[event] {
119			event = eventOther
120		}
121		return fanoutengine.Envelope{
122			Event:      event,
123			DeliveryID: ev.DeliveryID(),
124			ObservedAt: ev.Timestamp,
125			Body:       data,
126		}, nil
127	}
128	
129	// stampRefEventSpanAttrs stamps the envelope-level identity; the resolver adds
130	// the repo/ref attributes once it has re-decoded the body.
131	func stampRefEventSpanAttrs(span trace.Span, env fanoutengine.Envelope) {
132		span.SetAttributes(
133			attribute.String("entire.ref_event.op", env.Event),
134			attribute.String("entire.ref_event.delivery_id", env.DeliveryID),
135		)
136	}
137	
138	// nativeRouteResolver is the mirrorjobs.NativeMirrorResolver surface this
139	// consumer needs, narrowed for tests.
140	type nativeRouteResolver interface {
141		NativeMirrorRoutes(ctx context.Context, repoID string) (mirrorjobs.NativeMirrorResolution, error)
142	}
143	
144	// nativeMirrorSyncResolver resolves local ref events into mirror.git sync_repo
145	// routes, one per serving native mirror. It is the engine's Resolver for the
146	// native-mirror consumer.
147	//
148	// Loop prevention: a worker push into a native-mirror placement emits ref
149	// events on THAT cluster's repo_refs_v1 too. Those events resolve to a home
150	// cluster different from this consumer's local cluster and are dropped, so a
151	// sync can never trigger another sync. Only the home cluster — where user
152	// pushes land — fans out.
153	type nativeMirrorSyncResolver struct {
154		routes         nativeRouteResolver
155		localClusterID string
156	}
157	
158	func newNativeMirrorSyncResolver(routes nativeRouteResolver, localClusterID string) *nativeMirrorSyncResolver {
159		return &nativeMirrorSyncResolver{routes: routes, localClusterID: localClusterID}
160	}
161	
162	// Resolve returns one sync_repo route per serving mirror of the pushed repo.
163	// For a native-mirror group every ref op fans out — hash transitions move
164	// objects, and a symref_update (default-branch move) is reconciled by the
165	// worker's post-sync HEAD follow, the entiredb twin of the webhook path's
166	// default-branch edit. For a namespace group only refs under
167	// namespaceRefPrefix fan out; the rest of that repo's ref state belongs to
168	// GitHub's own mirroring. Transparency-log refs are skipped either way: every
169	// push writes them alongside the branch ref, so the branch event already
170	// triggers the (full-ref-state) sync.
171	func (d *nativeMirrorSyncResolver) Resolve(ctx context.Context, _ string, _ string, _ time.Time, body []byte) ([]fanoutengine.Route, string, error) {
172		ev, err := refevents.Unmarshal(body)
173		if err != nil {
174			// Unreachable in practice — Decode already validated this payload —
175			// kept as an input error so a future decoder/resolver drift Terms
176			// instead of redelivering a poison payload forever.
177			return nil, "", fanoutengine.Input("invalid ref event: %v", err)
178		}
179		if ev.RepoID == "" {
180			// Unmarshal tolerates absent fields by design (independent producer
181			// deploys), but an event with no repo id can never resolve — an
182			// input error (Term), not a Nak, or the poison payload would ride
183			// all MaxDeliver redeliveries for nothing.
184			return nil, "", fanoutengine.Input("ref event has no repo_id")
185		}
186	
187		if strings.HasPrefix(ev.RefName, "refs/tlog/") {
188			return nil, ackReasonTlogRef, nil
189		}
190	
191		// Stamp the parent span with the source coordinates so dropped or failed
192		// deliveries are still findable by repo id. entire.ref_event.op is
193		// re-stamped with the WIRE value: the decoder's envelope clamps unknown
194		// ops to "other" for metric cardinality, but the span can carry the
195		// real one.
196		span := trace.SpanFromContext(ctx)
197		span.SetAttributes(
198			attribute.String("entire.source_kind", "entiredb"),
199			attribute.String("entire.repo_id", ev.RepoID),
200			attribute.String("entire.ref_name", ev.RefName),
201			attribute.String("entire.ref_event.op", ev.RefOp),
202		)
203	
204		res, err := d.routes.NativeMirrorRoutes(ctx, ev.RepoID)
205		if err != nil {
206			if errors.Is(err, mirrorjobs.ErrNativeRepoNotFound) {
207				// Repo deleted between event publish and consume: benign skip.

content.content:
# mirror-pipeline

Services that synchronize GitHub repositories into Entire storage, plus the
shared code that binds them to a single protocol contract.

```
                                                        ┌──► cmd/fanout ───────────► NATS mirror_git_v1 ──► cmd/worker ──► entiredb receive-pack
                                                        │      (git-sync routes)      (per region)            │
GitHub webhook ──► cmd/webhook-ingest ──► NATS          ├──► cmd/meta-fanout ───────► NATS github_meta_v1 / github_pr_v1
                     (HMAC verify)        webhooks_github_v1  (display metadata, PRs)
                                                        ├──► cmd/core-fanout ───────► NATS github_push_author_v1
                                                        │      (push authors)
                                                        └──► cmd/trails-fanout ─────► NATS trail_forge_events_v1
                                                               (provider-neutral trail triggers)
```

Each consumer on `webhooks_github_v1` is an independent durable: every one
gets every delivery matching its subject filter, and a message is reclaimed
only when all matching durables have acked it. The worker records terminal
sync failures in a KV failure index;
`cmd/rekicker` re-drives those on a cron cadence.

## Services

- `cmd/webhook-ingest/` — verifies GitHub HMAC and publishes raw forwarded
  webhooks to `webhooks_github_v1`. Stateless; horizontally scalable.
- `cmd/fanout/` — resolves Git mirror routes for `push` events via
  entire-core and publishes target-owned sync jobs onto `mirror_git_v1`
  (cross-region in multi-region mode).
- `cmd/meta-fanout/` — fans out GitHub display metadata (`github_meta`) and
  pull-request (`github_pr`) jobs; also runs the backfill work-queue
  consumers and the resource-lifecycle fan.
- `cmd/core-fanout/` — extracts push authors from `push` events and publishes
  `github_push_author` jobs. Exhausted/malformed deliveries are captured to
  webhooks_github_dlq and Term'd (gated on ENTIRE_WEBHOOK_DLQ_ENABLED, same
  shape as cmd/fanout, pod-crash advisory backstop included).
- `cmd/trails-fanout/` — projects pull-request events (`opened`, `reopened`,
  `ready_for_review`, `closed`, `edited`), branch updates/deletions, and completed check
  suites into provider-neutral, placement-routed `trail_forge` events for
  entire-api. Check-suite refs are forge-reported candidates; entire-api must
  certify the exact ref/SHA against canonical EntireDB state. Our own family's
  suites (gate/status output) are dropped at the border before publishing —
  matched against the stable numeric App IDs in `ENTIRE_INTERNAL_GITHUB_APP_IDS`
  (prod, staging, ...) — so they never enter the per-cell stream and cannot
  re-trigger a gate off our own check run. Event arms land only alongside their
  entire-api handlers: the destination stream is WorkQueue-retained, so
  publishing an unhandled arm early would acknowledge and lose it. Its
  raw-webhook durables retry transient
  failures up to a bounded MaxDeliver and then, on exhaustion, capture the
  delivery to webhooks_github_dlq and Term it (gated on ENTIRE_WEBHOOK_DLQ_ENABLED,
  same as cmd/fanout) so a sustained outage doesn't silently drop trail events;
  malformed input still terminates immediately (captured too).
- `cmd/worker/` — mirror-worker. Consumes mirror jobs, fetches from GitHub,
  pushes refs to entiredb; records terminal failures in the failure index and
  publishes completion events. See `cmd/worker/docs/mirror-sync-guide.md`.
- `cmd/rekicker/` — per-cluster CronJob that re-emits failure-index entries
  so terminally-failed repos are re-driven.
- `cmd/mirror-pipeline-admin/` — operator CLI (webhook redelivery, DLQ
  inspection/replay, failure-index ops, backfill queues). See
  `docs/runbooks/`.

Load-testing tools (local / staging only, not in `.buildkite/deployments.json`):
`cmd/loadgen`, `cmd/mockgithub`, `cmd/loadtest-jetstream` — see
`docs/loadtest-local.md`.

## Shared packages

- `pkg/gitjobs/`, `pkg/metajobs/`, `pkg/prjobs/`, `pkg/pushauthorjobs/`,
  `pkg/trailforgeevents/`, `pkg/donejobs/` — canonical job schemas + typed
  publishers for each stream (publish mechanics shared via
  `internal/natspub`).
- `pkg/webhookevents/` — raw GitHub webhook stream contract
  (`webhooks_github_v1`).
- `pkg/webhookdlq/` — webhook dead-letter capture + advisory backstop.
- `pkg/failindex/` — mirror-sync failure index (KV) shared by worker,
  rekicker, and the admin CLI.
- `pkg/fanoutengine/` — shared NATS-consumer runtime (fetch loop, worker
  pool, Ack/Nak/Term decision tree, DLQ hook) behind the fanout
  binaries.
- `pkg/otelsetup/` — shared OTel tracer/meter setup + baggage plumbing.
  (W3C trace-context propagation over NATS message headers comes from
  go-nuts `natsmsg`.)
- `internal/` — service plumbing: mirror route resolution (`mirrorjobs`),
  cross-region NATS transport (`natsregions`), the shared
  publish core (`natspub`), the health/HTTP runtime (`svchttp`), and build
  identity (`version`).

One Go module at the repo root; dependencies are resolved from `go.mod` and
`go.sum`. Each deployed binary has its own Dockerfile built with the monorepo
root as context.

## CI and deployment

Buildkite owns CI and deployment. `.deploy-authority` is the switch: it reads
`buildkite` today, and `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and `test.yml` both read
it and skip themselves while it does. The GitHub Actions workflows are kept as
a tested rollback path, not as a second pipeline — see
`docs/runbooks/deploys.md` for how to flip back.

- `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` — runs `.buildkite/verify.sh` on every branch, then
  uploads the deployment graph on main.
- `.buildkite/verify.sh` — installs the pinned toolchain and mints the
  short-lived GitHub credential needed for private Go modules, then runs
  `scripts/ci/verify.sh`.
- `scripts/ci/verify.sh` — build, vet, race tests, gofmt check, lint. Both CI
  systems terminate here, so the checks themselves cannot drift.
- `.buildkite/deploy.py` — renders and runs the per-service graph
  (`staging: <svc>` then `production: <svc>`) from
  `.buildkite/deployments.json`, the single source of truth for the 8 deployed
  services and their images, dockerfiles, and Fleet overlays.

`mise run build|test|lint` runs the same tasks locally that
`scripts/ci/verify.sh` runs in CI.

`go.sum`. Each deployed binary has its own Dockerfile built with the monorepo
root as context.

## CI and deployment

Buildkite owns CI and deployment. `.deploy-authority` is the switch: it reads
`buildkite` today, and `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and `test.yml` both read
it and skip themselves while it does. The GitHub Actions workflows are kept as
a tested rollback path, not as a second pipeline — see
`docs/runbooks/deploys.md` for how to flip back.

- `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` — runs `.buildkite/verify.sh` on every branch, then
  uploads the deployment graph on main.
- `.buildkite/verify.sh` — installs the pinned toolchain and mints the
  short-lived GitHub credential needed for private Go modules, then runs
  `scripts/ci/verify.sh`.
- `scripts/ci/verify.sh` — build, vet, race tests, gofmt check, lint. Both CI
  systems terminate here, so the checks themselves cannot drift.
- `.buildkite/deploy.py` — renders and runs the per-service graph
  (`staging: <svc>` then `production: <svc>`) from
  `.buildkite/deployments.json`, the single source of truth for the 8 deployed
  services and their images, dockerfiles, and Fleet overlays.

`mise run build|test|lint` runs the same tasks locally that
`scripts/ci/verify.sh` runs in CI.
